**The Tackle Box**

The tackle box was the only thing his father had specified by name. Everything else — the house, the truck, the accounts with their modest balances — had been divided by percentages, the way lawyers prefer. But there was a line near the bottom of the second page: *The green Plano tackle box in the garage goes to Daniel.* As though someone might have contested it.

Daniel hadn't fished since he was eleven. He remembered the last time mostly as a feeling: the boat rocking, his father's silence, the way the lake gave back the sky so completely that it seemed rude to disturb it with a line. He'd asked to go home early. His father had said fine, and they'd never gone again, and neither of them had ever mentioned it, which was how most things went in that family.

The box was where the will said it would be, on the second shelf above the workbench, between a coffee can of screws and a dead car battery his father had apparently been saving for some reason. It was heavier than Daniel expected. He set it on the bench and unlatched it, and the trays rose up on their hinges the way they always had, a little mechanical flourish that had delighted him as a boy.

Lures. Dozens of them, most still carrying the faint smell of the lake. Rubber worms gone stiff. A spool of line yellowed to the color of old teeth. He recognized a red-and-white Daredevle spoon he'd once snagged in a submerged log and been sure he'd lost forever; his father had waded in to his waist to get it back, cursing quietly, and then said nothing about it for the rest of the day.

Under the bottom tray, where the box was deepest, there was a folded piece of paper. Lined, torn from a spiral notebook, soft from handling. Daniel unfolded it expecting a receipt or a fishing license, and instead found a list, in his father's square, engineer's printing.

*Things I should have said.*

Then, numbered:

*1. The ice cream was fine. I was mad about something else.*

*2. You were right about the dog.*

*3. I did read the story you wrote in 8th grade. I read it three times. I didn't know what to say so I said nothing and that was wrong.*

*4. I don't actually like fishing that much. I liked that you came.*

*5. When you moved to Denver I drove past your old school every day for a month. I don't know why I'm telling you that. I don't know why I'm not telling you that.*

*6.*

The sixth line was blank. Just the number, and the period, and then the blue rule of the paper running on to the edge.

Daniel read it twice. Then he sat down on the overturned bucket his father had used as a stool, because standing suddenly seemed like a lot to ask of himself.

The ice cream. He'd been seven, maybe eight. He'd dropped a cone in the parking lot of a Dairy Queen and his father had gone silent in the truck, the whole drive home, and Daniel had spent thirty years assuming he'd done something unforgivable with two dollars' worth of soft serve. And it had been something else. Of course it had been something else. His father had been a man made almost entirely of something else.

The dog was easier. Daniel had wanted to keep a stray that turned up when he was twelve. His father had said no, and then said no again, and then a week later the dog was gone. Daniel had assumed the pound. He'd been right about the dog. He didn't know, now, what he'd been right about — that it was gentle, that it would have been good for them, that it would have given them something to talk about on those long silent drives. All of it, maybe.

The story in eighth grade had been about a boy who could talk to rivers. Daniel had forgotten he'd written it until this moment, and now he could remember the last line, and the smell of the mimeograph paper, and handing it to his father at the dinner table and watching him fold it into his shirt pocket without a word.

*I didn't know what to say so I said nothing and that was wrong.*

He turned the paper over. The back was blank. He held it up to the bare bulb over the bench as though there might be something written in a lighter pencil, a seventh item, a signature. There wasn't.

He thought about what the sixth thing might have been. There were obvious candidates, the ones you'd expect at the end of a list like this — the three-word one, the one that fathers in movies manage while the music swells. Maybe his father had gotten that far, sat with the pen over the paper, and found that even in private, even in the garage with the door down, he couldn't put it in writing. Or maybe the sixth thing was smaller and stranger than that. *I liked your wife better than I let on. I was proud of the Denver thing. I'm scared.*

Or maybe the blank was the point. Maybe he'd left it open because he intended to keep adding, and then ran out of the one thing you can't buy more of at the hardware store.

Daniel folded the paper along its old creases and put it back under the tray, where it had been. He closed the box and latched it. Then he opened it again and took the paper out and put it in his shirt pocket, and it occurred to him that this was exactly what his father had done with the river story, and that maybe it hadn't been dismissal after all. Maybe it had just been a man putting something close to his heart the only way he knew how, which was the way you'd put away anything you meant to keep.

He carried the box out to his car. On the way, he passed the dead battery on the shelf and almost laughed, because he understood, suddenly, that his father had kept it for no reason at all — that some things you just don't get around to letting go of — and that this, too, was a kind of message, and probably the truest one in the garage.
